name: Semantic Layers
title: Semantic Layers
answer: A semantic layer defines business terms, metrics and relationships on top of raw tables, so that revenue or active customer means one agreed thing. Text to SQL systems that use one produce far more consistent answers than systems reading raw column names. It acts as a shared contract between data producers and consumers, separating business logic from physical storage. This reduces ambiguity in queries and lets analysts, dashboards and AI assistants reuse the same definitions.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A semantic layer usually runs as a service or embedded library between a data warehouse and the applications that query it. It stores metric definitions, joins and access rules in a metadata repository, often backed by a relational database such as PostgreSQL. It compiles requests into warehouse specific SQL and may cache results for repeated queries. Many implementations are now exposed through Model Context Protocol servers, and this site tracks 262 active MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with data modelers defining dimensions, measures, filters and relationships in a version controlled specification, often written in YAML or a dedicated modeling language. That specification is validated against the underlying schema and compiled into SQL at query time. Semantic layers also resolve joins, apply time zone and currency conversions, and enforce row level security. Teams review metric changes through pull requests and test definitions against sample data before publishing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who can define, change and access each metric. Effective governance records provenance for every definition, including its owner, last change and source tables, so an incorrect number can be traced. Access controls are applied at the semantic object level, not just the table level, which limits exposure of sensitive fields. The main risk is that a poorly governed layer becomes a single point of failure, where one bad definition propagates across many reports and AI answers. Regular review and clear ownership reduce that risk.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Semantic layers are moving closer to AI assistants and agents, where they act as the trusted context for text to SQL and retrieval. The growth of Model Context Protocol servers, with 2401 active servers tracked on this site, suggests that semantic definitions will be shared across many tools rather than locked in one platform. Future work is likely to combine semantic layers with active metadata, automated metric testing and natural language query interfaces. The goal is a single governed layer that both humans and machines query through the same business language.
